name: The Maillard reaction — browning is a flavor factory
scope: The reaction that turns pale food brown, roasty and savory. T1: a seared steak, toast, and roasted coffee taste completely different from their pale or boiled selves because BROWNING builds brand-new flavors — it is not just 'more cooked.' T2: the toasty flavor of a steak crust, browned toast, roasted coffee, and fried onions is all the SAME chemistry — heat making sugars react with proteins/amino acids (the Maillard reaction). T3: it only fires above the boiling point of water, which is why anything wet or boiled stays pale (its surface is stuck near 100 C) and only a dry, hot surface browns. T4: the brown color itself comes from big new molecules (melanoidins) formed right alongside the aromas — color and flavor are born together. T5: it is named for Louis-Camille Maillard, the French chemist who first described it in 1912 (food-history beat). Extra rungs for depth: alkaline conditions turbo-charge it into deep mahogany, which is why a pretzel or bagel is dipped in a baking-soda/lye bath before baking (its dark glossy skin is amped-up Maillard); browned onions go sweet-and-savory because their sugars AND proteins react; patting food dry first browns it faster because no energy is wasted boiling off surface water; a milk-or-sugar brush (egg wash, honey) browns a crust faster.
source: Wikipedia 'Maillard reaction' (named for Louis-Camille Maillard, described 1912, 140-165 C / 280-330 F, amino acid + reducing sugar, melanoidins); C&EN 'The Maillard Reaction Turns 100' (2012); Harold McGee, On Food and Cooking (alkaline browning of pretzels/bagels). Grokipedia 'Maillard_reaction' attempted first (fetch blocked, HTTP 403).
framing_note: Scene-led — open on the smell/look of a specific browned food, never 'What is the Maillard reaction?' Every answer names a concrete browning fact (a food, the alkaline pretzel trick, the melanoidin color molecule, the 1912 origin). Accuracy rail: Maillard needs sugar + protein/amino acids AND above-boiling heat — keep it cleanly distinct from caramelization (sugar alone). Do NOT test the 140-165 C number as an answer (banned minutiae); it may be context/distractor only. Dinner-test payoff rung: the pretzel/bagel alkaline-bath rung — its deep-brown skin is Maillard turned up.

name: Dry heat vs wet heat — matching the method to the cut
scope: Why the same trick that perfects a steak ruins a brisket. T1: a butcher's 'tough' cuts (chuck, shank, brisket, shoulder) come from hard-working muscles, while 'tender' cuts (loin, tenderloin, rib) come from muscles that barely move — the hard-workers are packed with chewy connective tissue. T2: you cook them oppositely — tender cuts get fast, dry, high heat (sear, grill, roast, broil, fry); tough cuts get slow, low, wet heat (braise, stew, simmer, poach). T3: the reason is that connective tissue — long moist heat melts it into silky richness, while fast dry heat just makes a tough cut tougher and drier. T4: it runs backward too — braise a lean tenderloin and you RUIN it (it has almost no connective tissue to melt, so it just dries out and goes gray); a filet wants seconds of fierce heat, not hours in a pot. T5 (payoff): wet heat cannot brown at all (it is capped near boiling, ~100 C, and browning needs hotter) — so a proper braise is SEARED dry and hot FIRST, then simmered, to get both crust-flavor and fall-apart tenderness. Extra rungs: steaming and poaching are the gentlest wet heat, saved for the most delicate foods (fish, eggs); a quick 'which cut, which method' pairing (chuck roast to the braise, ribeye to the grill).
source: ScienceOfCooking.com 'Science of Slow Cooking'; Meathead / AmazingRibs 'Basic Meat Science For Cooks'; Chef Approved Tools 'Braising 101' (tough cuts = high-connective-tissue, moist heat; wet heat capped ~100 C). Grokipedia 'Braising' / 'Cooking' consulted; corroborated by listed sources.
framing_note: Scene-led on a real named cut and a real pot or pan, never 'define dry vs wet heat.' Answers are concrete cut+method facts. Accuracy rails: tough cuts = hard-working muscles high in connective tissue -> moist heat; braising a lean tender cut RUINS it; wet heat maxes near 100 C so it cannot brown. Prep-frame ('you sear it, you braise it') is fine; keep any butchery wording matter-of-fact for a kid. Payoff rung: the reversal (T4) — why you must NOT braise a filet.

name: "Searing seals in the juices" — the great cooking myth
scope: The most-repeated wrong thing in cooking. T1: many cooks say you sear a steak to 'seal in the juices' and trap moisture inside — this is FALSE. T2: seared and un-seared roasts lose about the same amount of juice; the brown crust is not waterproof — the sizzling you hear the whole time IS moisture escaping and vaporizing. T3 (payoff): searing is absolutely worth doing, but for FLAVOR, not moisture — the browned crust is the Maillard reaction, a taste upgrade, not a seal. T4: the myth even has an author — 19th-century chemist Justus von Liebig proposed the 'searing seals the juices' idea (1847), and it was believed for nearly a century until simple experiments in the 1930s disproved it. Extra rung: fierce searing heat actually dries the surface MORE, not less, because moisture loss rises with temperature.
source: Meathead / AmazingRibs 'Myth: Searing Steaks Seals In The Juices'; Harold McGee, On Food and Cooking ('the biggest myth in cooking'; crust is not waterproof); TodayIFoundOut 'Searing Meat Does Not Seal in the Juices' (Liebig 1847, disproven 1930s). Grokipedia 'Searing' consulted; corroborated by listed sources.
framing_note: Scene-led on the sizzling pan, never a bare 'true or false: searing seals juices' definition. The T1 stem can voice the myth as a character's belief so all four choices stay live and the player must KNOW the truth, not deduce it. Accuracy rail: searing does NOT retain moisture; it browns for flavor (Maillard). Payoff rung: what searing REALLY does — builds flavor, not a seal (T3).

name: Don't crowd the pan — brown vs steam
scope: Why the same mushrooms come out golden one time and gray-rubbery the next. T1: pile a pan too full and the food comes out pale, gray and rubbery instead of browned — the classic crowded-pan fail. T2: cold, wet food releases water as it heats; when the pan is packed, that steam has nowhere to escape, so the food STEAMS in its own moisture instead of browning. T3 (payoff): browning (Maillard) needs the surface hotter than boiling, but a steamy, crowded pan is stuck near 100 C — it physically cannot brown until the water is gone. T4: the fixes all keep the surface dry and hot — pat the food dry, use a bigger pan, and cook in batches with space between the pieces. Extra rung: this is exactly why a big batch of meat for a stew is seared a few pieces at a time before it ever meets the liquid.
source: Cross-checked against Maillard sources above (surface must exceed ~100 C to brown) and Meathead / AmazingRibs cooking-science articles; standard culinary technique (Kenji Lopez-Alt / Serious Eats 'don't crowd the pan'). Grokipedia 'Sauteing' consulted; corroborated by listed sources.
framing_note: Scene-led on mushrooms or meat going gray, never 'define overcrowding.' Answers are concrete pan-behavior facts. Accuracy rail: crowding traps steam, so the surface cannot exceed ~100 C and Maillard cannot start. Prep-frame ('you crowd the pan') is fine. Payoff rung: WHY it steams instead of browns — the surface is pinned at boiling temperature (T3).

name: The screaming-hot pan and the dancing droplet (Leidenfrost)
scope: Why chefs heat a pan empty and flick water at it. T1: good cooks heat a pan HOT before the food goes in — a cold pan gives you pale, stuck, steamed food instead of a sear. T2: a preheated pan holds stored-up heat (thermal mass), so it does not crash cold when the food lands — it keeps searing instead of stalling. T3: there is a classic readiness test — flick a few drops of water in; if they instantly hiss away the pan is not ready, but if they gather into beads that skitter and glide around the surface, it is hot enough. T4 (payoff): those dancing beads are the Leidenfrost effect — the pan is so hot (around 400 F / 200 C) that the underside of each drop flashes to steam and lifts the drop on a thin cushion of vapor, so it glides almost frictionlessly before it finally evaporates. Extra rung: the same effect is why a wet fingertip can tap a screaming-hot surface unharmed for a split second — the vapor layer briefly protects it.
source: ScienceABC 'The Leidenfrost Effect'; Kiddle 'Leidenfrost effect facts for kids' (vapor cushion; ~193-200 C for water on metal, well above 100 C boiling). Grokipedia 'Leidenfrost_effect' consulted; corroborated by listed sources.
framing_note: Scene-led on the water skittering across the pan, never 'what is the Leidenfrost effect?' INVERT THE WONDER: put the marvel (drops that dance and refuse to die) in the STEM and make the named effect/mechanism the answer. Accuracy rail: Leidenfrost needs the surface WELL above boiling (~200 C for water); the drop rides its own steam cushion. Payoff rung: the dancing-droplet Leidenfrost reveal (T4).

name: Carryover cooking and resting meat
scope: Why a roast keeps cooking after it leaves the oven. T1: pull a roast at exactly your target doneness and it ends up OVERcooked — the inside keeps climbing for several minutes on the counter. T2: that is carryover cooking — the hot outer layers are still far hotter than the center, and that stored heat keeps flowing inward after you take the meat off the heat. T3 (payoff): so you pull the meat BEFORE it hits target — roughly 5 F early for a steak, up to 10-15 F early for a big roast — and let it coast up to temperature while it rests. T4: resting does a second job — straight off the heat the muscle fibers are clenched and juice floods out the moment you cut; a few minutes' rest lets them relax and reabsorb juice, so it stays in the meat. Extra rung: size drives it — a thin steak carries over only a few degrees, a huge roast or turkey up to 15 F, so bigger cuts get pulled earlier.
source: Wikipedia 'Carryover cooking'; ThermoWorks 'Resting: The Final Phase of Cooking'; Meathead / AmazingRibs 'Carryover Cooking' (internal temp rises ~5-15 F by size; juice redistribution on resting). Grokipedia 'Carryover_cooking' consulted; corroborated by listed sources.
framing_note: Scene-led on the roast overshooting on the counter, never 'define carryover cooking.' Answers are concrete temperature/resting facts. Accuracy rail: carryover raises internal temp ~5-15 F depending on size -> pull early; resting lets juices redistribute (redistribution is standard; do not overstate it as 'no juice loss'). Payoff rung: the pull-it-early rule (T3).

name: Fond, deglaze, and the pan sauce
scope: The brown, stuck-on gold at the bottom of the pan. T1: after you sear meat, the pan bottom is crusted with brown stuck-on bits — beginners scrub them away as 'burnt,' but they are pure concentrated flavor. T2: those browned bits have a name — fond (French for 'bottom' or 'base') — and they are the very same Maillard flavor as the crust on the meat, just glued to the metal. T3 (payoff): you pour in a splash of liquid (wine, stock, even water) and scrape while it bubbles — the fond dissolves off the metal into the liquid; that move is called deglazing. T4: the deglazed, flavor-loaded liquid becomes the base of a pan sauce or gravy — the whole point is that none of that browned flavor gets wasted. Extra rungs: acidic liquids like wine or a splash of vinegar lift fond especially well; the one time you DO throw it out is when the fond is black and bitter — that is burnt, not browned.
source: Chowhound 'What It Means To Deglaze Your Pan's Fond'; Offcuts Kitchen 'What Is Fond' (fond = French 'stock/base/bottom', formed by Maillard); MasterClass 'How to Deglaze a Pan'. Grokipedia 'Deglazing' consulted; corroborated by listed sources.
framing_note: Scene-led on the crusty pan right after searing, never 'define fond/deglaze.' Answers name the concrete thing (fond, the deglaze move, the resulting sauce). Accuracy rail: fond = browned (Maillard) bits, flavor not garbage; deglazing dissolves it with liquid; only truly BURNT/black fond is discarded. Prep-frame voice ('you deglaze the pan') is welcome. Payoff rung: the deglaze move that turns stuck bits into a sauce (T3).

name: Reduction — boiling flavor down
scope: How a thin, watery sauce becomes thick, glossy and intense. T1: simmer a sauce or stock uncovered and it slowly shrinks, thickens, turns glossy, and tastes far more intense — you added nothing, you took water away. T2: that is a reduction — water leaves as steam while the flavor, sugar and body stay behind and concentrate. T3 (payoff): a long-reduced stock becomes a syrupy, spoon-coating glaze (a demi-glace), and balsamic vinegar reduces to a sweet syrup — the shine and thickness are concentrated dissolved solids, not added flour or thickener. T4: reduction concentrates SALT too, so you season at the END — salt a sauce before reducing it and it can finish far too salty. Extra rung: covering the pot stops a reduction (trapped steam just drips back in), which is why you always reduce UNcovered.
source: FlavoryCooking 'Mastering the Art of Reduction'; NovaChef 'Reduction Sauces - Meat Glaze - Glace' (evaporation concentrates flavor and salt; demi-glace); Reluctant Gourmet 'How to Make a Reduction Sauce'. Grokipedia 'Reduction_(cooking)' consulted; corroborated by listed sources.
framing_note: Scene-led on the shrinking, thickening, glossy sauce, never 'define reduction.' Answers are concrete facts about concentrating flavor. Accuracy rail: reduction removes water by evaporation and concentrates flavor AND salt — season last; it thickens without added starch. Payoff rung: the salt trap — season at the end (T4).

name: Oil smoke points — why butter burns but ghee doesn't
scope: Choosing the right fat for the heat. T1: push a fat too far and it starts to smoke, smells acrid, and makes food taste burnt and bitter — every fat has a temperature where this begins. T2: that temperature is the smoke point, and it differs for every fat, so you match the fat to the job — a gentle one for a low saute, a tough one for a screaming sear. T3: butter smokes surprisingly LOW (around 300 F / 150 C) — not because of its fat, but because of the little bits of milk solids (proteins and sugars) suspended in it, which scorch. T4 (payoff): skim those milk solids out and you get clarified butter, or ghee, which takes much higher heat (around 450 F / 230 C and up) — same buttery flavor, no burning. T5: this is why you do not sear a steak in extra-virgin olive oil (lower smoke point, and its delicate flavor is wasted at high heat) but reach for a refined high-smoke-point oil like avocado for a hard sear. Extra rung: refining an oil (stripping out its impurities) is exactly what raises its smoke point.
source: Wikipedia 'Template:Smoke point of cooking oils'; The Kitchn 'What Is Smoke Point'; VomFass 'Smoke Point of Oils Chart' (butter ~300-350 F from milk solids; ghee ~450 F; refined avocado highest; EVOO ~325-410 F). Grokipedia 'Smoke_point' consulted; corroborated by listed sources.
framing_note: Scene-led on butter foaming, then browning, then burning, never 'define smoke point.' Answers are concrete fat facts. Accuracy rail: butter's LOW smoke point comes from its MILK SOLIDS; clarifying (ghee) removes them and raises it — do NOT say the butterfat itself is the weak link. Exact temperatures are context, not the tested answer. Payoff rung: ghee = butter minus the burnable milk solids (T4).

name: Simmer vs rolling boil — gentle vs violent water
scope: The classic 'crank it up so it cooks hotter' mistake. T1: a simmer is a few small bubbles lazily breaking the surface; a rolling boil is big, fast, roiling bubbles and clouds of steam. T2 (payoff): cranking the heat to a hard boil does NOT make the water hotter — at sea level both a simmer and a rolling boil sit at about 212 F / 100 C; the boil is just far more violent agitation, not more heat. T3: so you match the violence to the food — a bare simmer for delicate things (poached eggs, fish, a clear stock) because a rolling boil would batter them apart and turn stock cloudy; a hard boil for pasta, where the churning keeps the strands from clumping. T4: poaching is gentler still, below a simmer (water barely trembling), for the most fragile foods. Extra rung: a hard boil boils the water AWAY faster (more steam) but does not cook the food's interior any faster than a simmer.
source: Taste of Home 'Boil vs Simmer'; Sur La Table / Lid & Ladle 'Simmer vs Boil' (both ~100 C at sea level; difference is agitation; simmer/poach for delicate foods). Grokipedia 'Simmering' / 'Boiling' consulted; corroborated by listed sources.
framing_note: Scene-led on the two pots side by side, never 'define simmer vs boil.' Answers are concrete water-behavior facts. Accuracy rail: at sea level both sit at ~100 C — a rolling boil is NOT hotter, only more agitated (state 'at sea level' since altitude lowers the boiling point). Payoff rung: the misconception-buster — boiling is not hotter than simmering (T2).

name: Deep frying — why hot oil cooks dry, not greasy
scope: The counterintuitive truth about fried food. T1: fry food in oil that is hot ENOUGH and it comes out crisp and barely greasy; fry it in oil that is too cool and it comes out pale, soggy and oil-logged — so hotter oil actually means LESS greasy. T2: when food hits hot oil, the water just under its surface flashes to steam and rushes outward — that furious outward rush is the violent bubbling you see. T3 (payoff): that outward blast of steam is a barrier that physically holds the oil OUT so it cannot soak in — but only while the food is hot enough to keep steaming; cool oil means weak steam, and the oil creeps in and turns the food greasy. T4: the crisp golden shell forms once the surface has dried out and begins to brown (Maillard plus crisped starch). Extra rung: fried food goes greasy if it sits and cools on the plate, because the steam inside condenses back to water and can pull oil in — which is why fries are best straight from the fryer.
source: Wikipedia 'Deep frying'; HomeCookingTech 'The Science Behind Deep Frying'; My German Table 'Why deep-frying at lower temperatures doesn't make food oily' (outward steam barrier repels oil; cool oil -> greasy). Grokipedia 'Deep_frying' consulted; corroborated by listed sources.
framing_note: Scene-led on the furious bubbling of fresh fries, never 'define deep frying.' Answers are concrete frying-physics facts. Accuracy rail: hot-enough oil creates an OUTWARD steam barrier that keeps oil out; cool oil makes food greasy — counterintuitive but correct. Payoff rung: the steam-barrier reveal — hotter oil is less greasy (T3).

name: Three ways heat travels — grill, pan, oven
scope: Why the same steak cooks differently on a grill, in a skillet, and in an oven — the heat reaches it three different ways. T1: a steak on a grill, in a pan, and in an oven cooks differently even at the 'same' temperature, because the heat gets to the food by three different routes. T2: a skillet cooks by direct contact — hot metal touching the food (conduction) — and that tight contact is why a pan delivers the hardest, fastest sear. T3: an oven cooks mostly through hot air moving around the food (convection) — gentler and all-around, which is why it is for roasting and baking, not an instant sear. T4 (payoff): a grill or broiler cooks largely by radiant heat thrown from glowing coals or a hot element (radiation) — like the warmth of the sun — and the dark stripes (grill marks) are where the hot metal bars touched directly (conduction) while the gaps between stayed paler. Extra rung: a convection OVEN adds a fan to push the hot air around faster, so it cooks more evenly and a bit quicker than a still oven.
source: Wikipedia 'Heat transfer' and 'Grilling' (conduction/convection/radiation applied to cooking appliances); standard culinary-science references (McGee, On Food and Cooking). Grokipedia 'Heat_transfer' consulted; corroborated by listed sources.
framing_note: Scene-led on the same steak in three appliances, never a bare 'define conduction/convection/radiation' quiz. Anchor every answer to a real appliance and what it does to the food — the physics term is the payoff, not a memorized definition. Accuracy rail: pan = conduction, oven = convection, grill/broiler = radiation (plus conduction at the bars). Payoff rung: why grill marks are striped (T4).
